1) the majority of autistic individuals have friends; 2) autistic children and adolescents are able to form friendships with both autistic and non autistic children and adolescents; 3) the majority of friendships formed by autistic adolescents are with non autistic adolescents; 4) the majority of social relationships formed by autistic adults are with other autistic adults; 5) autistic individuals who form social relationships with non autistic peers are more likely to be satisfied with their social relationships than autistic individuals who only form social relationships

In summary, our research is concerned with
establishing the foundations of successful friendships and social relationships in the autism way.
the development of a model of social inclusion that is informed by the needs and perspectives of autistic children and adults.
understanding the social relationships and experiences of autistic individuals, and how we might best support them to develop and maintain friendships and relationships with others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
autistic individuals do want friends. They just need support to find them and maintain them.
autistic children and adolescents want friendships and relationships, but that these relationships need to be developed in a way that is consistent with their individual needs and interests.

autistic individuals do not lack the desire for social interaction, but rather, they may have difficulties in understanding the rules and nuances of social interaction, and therefore, may not always know how to engage in social interactions in a way that leads to successful outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social inclusion for autistic people is possible and that it is possible to establish social inclusion the autism way.
social relationships are a critical component to the quality of life for individuals with autism.
autistic people are capable of developing meaningful relationships with neurotypical people, but that the environment must be conducive to support these relationships to form.
The main takeaway from our work is that
autistic children and young people do want to form friendships and that the right environment can help them do so.
autistic children and adolescents are not averse to social interaction and relationships with others.
autistic individuals want friends and are capable of forming meaningful friendships and social relationships with others.
